title: flowers on the man who lost
hookLine: the war is won, the teacher raises his plough at the winner, and flowers fall on the man who lost
carry: svadharma: even Duryodhana's courage is counted

cards: Duryodhana lies on the ground and can't get up. The fight is over. The Pandavas have won the war.
And for a moment, nobody behaves the way winners are supposed to. Bhima walks over to the fallen king and puts his foot on his head. Yudhishthira, his own brother, tells him to stop.
And Balarama, the teacher who trained both fighters, is so angry at the blow he just saw that he lifts his plough, his own weapon, and runs at Bhima. The victory itself is put on trial.

teach.b: In Ganguli's telling, Yudhishthira tells Bhima the foot does him no honor.
Krishna catches hold of Balarama and reminds him of Bhima's vow from the dice hall, but Balarama leaves for Dvaraka in anger.

Then the fallen king turns on Krishna and lists the deaths he calls unfair: Bhishma, Drona, Karna. Krishna answers with a list of his own: the poison, the house of lac, the dice, Draupadi dragged into the hall.
Your own wrongs brought you here. Duryodhana answers that he lived as a king should: he ruled, he gave, he fought and never ran. And flowers rain down on him from the sky.
Music sounds. The Pandavas stand there downcast. Here's the teaching under the flowers.

Hindus speak of svadharma, your own dharma, the duty that belongs to your place in life. For a warrior, the Gita says, death in battle opens heaven. Duryodhana did terrible wrong, and his wrongs brought him down.
But he also kept a warrior's dharma to the very end, and the epic counts that too.
At the close of the whole Mahabharata, Yudhishthira reaches heaven and is furious to find Duryodhana already there, and he's told this is why. The epic won't let anyone be only a villain.
Most of us keep a short list of people we've cast as the bad guy. The Hindu view doesn't erase what they did; it asks you to see the dharma they kept as well.

how: The mace fight and its aftermath are told in recitations and retellings of the Mahabharata, and some retellings give Duryodhana a measure of honor in defeat.

games.q: you're Narada, in heaven at the epic's end. Yudhishthira is angry to find Duryodhana already there. what do you tell him?
o: that it's a mistake, and Duryodhana will be sent away.
that Duryodhana kept a warrior's dharma to the end, and that is counted.
that heaven doesn't care what anyone did on earth.
games.why: Narada tells him Duryodhana won his place by the warrior's dharma, fighting without fear to the last. svadharma is counted, even in him.

practice: Bring your palms together at your heart, the way Hindus greet each other with namaste, bowing to what is sacred in the other person. Bring to mind someone you've filed as the villain of a story in your life.
Don't excuse what they did. Breathing in, name one thing they did rightly, one duty they kept. Breathing out, let both be true at once, the way the epic lets flowers fall on Duryodhana.
If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Shalya. The war's last book ends with a fallen king, two lists of wrongs, and flowers falling on the man who lost, for the dharma he kept.

orig.note: Balarama: Krishna's elder brother, who taught the mace to both Bhima and Duryodhana.

carryVoice: Your line: svadharma, even Duryodhana's courage is counted. Tomorrow, night falls on the field, and three men are left. See you then.
